kapak.alt: Acoustic and electric in one ear

youtube.baslik: Electric-Acoustic Stimulation (EAS) and Hybrid Systems | Lesson 245 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Can one ear receive both acoustic and electric stimulation when low-frequency hearing remains but the high frequencies are lost? In this lesson we cover the candidacy logic of electric-acoustic stimulation (EAS), hearing preservation surgery, how hearing preservation is classified, programming and expected outcomes.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: von Ilberg et al. (1999), Electric-acoustic stimulation of the auditory system, ORL; Gantz and Turner (2003), Combining acoustic and electrical hearing, Laryngoscope; Skarzynski et al. (2013), Towards a consensus on a hearing preservation classification system, Acta Oto-Laryngologica; Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Acoustic and electric in the same ear
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how one ear can receive both acoustic and electric stimulation when low-frequency hearing remains.
We will cover candidacy, hearing preservation surgery, programming and expected outcomes.
In this example, the right ear has a mild to moderate loss in the low frequencies and a profound loss in the high frequencies.
In steeply sloping losses like this, a hearing aid makes low sounds audible but often cannot make high-frequency consonants audible.
The person hears sounds but struggles to understand speech, especially in noise and with high-frequency consonants.
A standard cochlear implant conveys high frequencies well, but natural low-frequency hearing may be lost when the electrode is inserted.
Electric-acoustic stimulation, or EAS, aims to combine these two worlds in the same ear.
The high frequencies are stimulated electrically by the implant, and the low frequencies acoustically with amplified sound.
The values are only an example; the actual candidacy decision follows a full evaluation and a team discussion.
An EAS candidate has usable residual hearing in the low frequencies that can benefit from amplification.
For example, US approval studies required thresholds up to five hundred hertz no worse than about sixty to sixty five decibels HL.
In the mid and high frequencies, the loss is severe to profound.
With well-fitted hearing aids, word recognition benefit is limited; this is the same logic as standard implant candidacy.
Criteria vary by country, device and reimbursement rules; in Türkiye, the current Health Implementation Communiqué should be checked.
Whether the residual hearing is progressive also matters; with a rapidly progressing loss, preserved hearing may not last long.

cumleler.yazi: In 1999, von Ilberg and colleagues reported the first results combining electric and acoustic stimulation in the same ear.
cumleler.ses: In nineteen ninety nine, von Ilberg and colleagues reported the first results combining electric and acoustic stimulation in the same ear.

cumleler: Around the same time, Gantz and Turner tried to preserve low-frequency hearing with short electrodes placed only in the cochlear base.
In the years that followed, thin, flexible electrodes and surgical techniques that cause minimal cochlear damage were developed.
Today, in many systems the same processor delivers both the implant stimulation and acoustic sound into the ear canal.
Preserving residual hearing is now a goal not only for EAS candidates but in many standard implant surgeries as well.

sahneler.baslik: Electric at the base, acoustic at the *apex*
cumleler: The logic of EAS rests on the frequency map of the cochlea.
The hair cells at the base are largely lost; this region is stimulated electrically by the electrode array.
Near the apex, the hair cells largely still work; low sounds reach this region acoustically, through the traveling wave.
So the array is advanced in a way that does not damage this region; its length and insertion depth are chosen accordingly.
The electrode is usually inserted slowly through the round window, so as to cause minimal damage to the inner structures of the cochlea.
Two kinds of stimulation then work side by side in the same ear: electric for the highs, acoustic sound for the lows.
This graph shows the preserved low-frequency hearing of an example EAS user after surgery.
In the low frequencies, where acoustic amplification helps, sound is delivered into the ear canal through a receiver.
Higher frequencies are assigned to the electrodes and delivered electrically.
The point where the two regions meet is called the crossover frequency; it is chosen from the person's audiogram.
When setting the crossover, the aim is to avoid both overlap between the two kinds of stimulation and a gap between them.
The acoustic part is usually delivered by a small receiver linked to the same processor, with an earmold or an ear tip.
Hearing preservation requires as little trauma to the cochlea as possible; this is also called soft surgery.
The electrode is usually advanced very slowly and in a controlled way through the round window or a small nearby opening.
A thin, flexible electrode of suitable length lowers the chance of damaging the basilar membrane and inner structures.
Some centers use steroids around the time of surgery to protect the inner ear.
Monitoring the cochlear response with electrocochleography during surgery can show the surgeon a risk of damage in real time.
These techniques are chosen by the surgeon and the team; the audiologist measures hearing in detail before and after surgery.
Before surgery, low-frequency thresholds are measured in detail; in this example, the navy line shows the preoperative thresholds.
After surgery, thresholds are measured again; most people show some shift.
The size of the shift is calculated from the difference between the pre and postoperative low-frequency averages.

cumleler.yazi: The 2013 classification by Skarzynski and colleagues relates the shift to the residual hearing range and gives preservation as a percentage.
cumleler.ses: The twenty thirteen classification by Skarzynski and colleagues relates the shift to the residual hearing range and gives preservation as a percentage.

cumleler: Above seventy five percent is complete, twenty five to seventy five percent partial, and below twenty five percent minimal preservation.
If no measurable hearing remains, there is considered to be no preservation.
This shared language lets us compare the results of different centers and techniques; this example corresponds to partial preservation.
In some people, hearing that is preserved right after surgery may decline over months or years.
The cause is not fully known; tissue reaction in the inner ear and the natural progression of the loss are among the possible factors.
If low-frequency hearing declines, the map can be changed to send the low frequencies to the electrodes, with fully electric stimulation.
So some teams prefer an electrode that reaches a depth able to carry the low frequencies too, if needed.
Before surgery, the person is told clearly that the team will try to preserve residual hearing, but that this is not guaranteed.
EAS programming starts with a current audiogram at every visit, because the acoustic part is set directly from these thresholds.
The crossover frequency is chosen from the upper limit up to which low-frequency hearing can benefit from acoustic amplification.
The acoustic part is fitted like a hearing aid with a prescription formula and, if possible, verified with real ear measurement.
In the electric part, as with a standard implant, T and C or M levels are set.
Finally, we check whether the two parts sound natural and balanced together, and speech tests are done.
As residual hearing changes, the crossover frequency and acoustic gain are updated too.
Studies show that preserved low-frequency hearing contributes clearly to understanding speech, especially in noise.
This is explained by low-frequency pitch information helping to separate speech from the background.
In music listening, melody and timbre perception are usually better than with electric stimulation alone.
Users often find the sound more natural and less mechanical.
For many people, the benefit of acoustic and electric stimulation together exceeds that of either one alone.
The benefit varies from person to person and depends on how much hearing is preserved.

sahneler.metin: Remeasure low-frequency thresholds at every EAS visit. If thresholds have changed, update acoustic gain and crossover frequency the same day.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: at every visit, remeasure the low-frequency thresholds of the EAS user's implanted ear.
Missing a threshold change and keeping the old acoustic settings leads to either too little or too much low-frequency amplification.
If thresholds have worsened, update the acoustic gain and crossover frequency the same day, and explain the reason to the person.
Tell the person to contact the center without delay if they notice a sudden change in their hearing.

maddeler.metin: Candidate: low hearing present, high absent

cumleler: Electric-acoustic stimulation stimulates the high frequencies electrically and the low frequencies acoustically in the same ear.
The candidate has usable low-frequency hearing but a severe to profound loss in the high frequencies.
Hearing preservation surgery and electrode choice aim to keep low-frequency hearing; preservation may be complete, partial or minimal.
Preserved low-frequency hearing helps speech in noise, music and naturalness; thresholds are remeasured at every visit.

sahneler.soru: How are low frequencies delivered in EAS?
sahneler.aciklama: Residual low-frequency hearing is stimulated _acoustically_, the highs electrically.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in an EAS system, how are the low frequencies usually delivered?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: by acoustic amplification.
Preserved low-frequency hearing is stimulated with amplified sound in the ear canal; the high frequencies are assigned to the electrodes.
